§ 2Content

Basic Pointers:

  • Judiciary in India is Integrated (borrowed from GoI act of 1935) and Independent.
  • The Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court and the Judicial Committee of Privy Council after India gained Independence.
  • 1st sitting: 28 Jan, 1950
  • Federal Court was established in 1937 under the provisions of GoI Act 1935.
  • SC is also known as 'the Guardian of the Constitution.'

§ 3PART V - SUPREME COURT

Chapter IV: [Article 124-147]

Article 124 — Establishment and Constitution of Supreme Court

  1. 1. Strength of Judges
  • Originally, strength: 1 Chief Justice + 7 Judges = 8 Judges
  • Present, strength: 1 Chief Justice + 33 Judges = 34 Judges (Maximum sanctioned strength: 34)
  1. 2. Every judge of SC shall be appointed by the President after consultation with CJI.
  • Tenure: Serves till the age of 65 years, provided that—
  • (a) a Judge may resign his office by writing to the President.
  • (b) a Judge to be removed in the manner provided in clause (4).
  • 2(A) The age of a SC Judge to be determined in such manner as Parliament may by law provide. (15th CAA, 1963)
  1. 3. Qualification for SC Judges:
  • A Citizen of India.
  • (a) At least 5 years as a Judge of a High Court, or
  • (b) At least 10 years as an Advocate of a High Court, or
  • (c) Distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President.
  1. 4. Removal: A Judge can be removed by President after Parliament passes an address by Special Majority (i.e. majority of total membership + 2/3rd of members present and voting) on grounds of:
  • Proved misbehaviour or Incapacity
Procedure of Removal for Supreme Court/High Court Judges is mentioned in Judges Enquiry Act, 1968
Motion to remove judges should be signed by 50 members of Rajya Sabha or 100 members of Lok Sabha.
  1. 5. Parliament may by law establish procedure for investigating judge's misconduct as mentioned in clause (4).
  2. 6. A Judge of SC to subscribe an Oath or affirmation before the President.
  3. 7. Restrictions: After retirement, a SC judge cannot practice law in any court within the territory of India.

Collegium System

(Not mentioned in Constitution.)

It is a system under which appointments and transfers of judges are decided by a forum of the CJI and the 4 senior most judges of the Supreme Court. It has no place in the Indian constitution. Its origin can be traced from the following judges cases:

First Judges Case (1982 - S.P. Gupta Case):

  • Recommendation of CJI not binding on the President.
  • Gave primacy to the executive in judicial appointments.

Second Judges Case (1993):

  • Introduced the Collegium system, holding that "Consultation" means Concurrence.
  • Recommendation made by CJI + 2 senior-most judges.
  • Recommendation given by CJI will be binding on President.

Third Judges Case (1998):

  • Collegium expanded to a 5 member body.
  • CJI + 4 senior-most judges, decision binding on the President.
The Parliament replaced the collegium system by National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) through 99th CA, 2014 to provide recommendations to the President.

Fourth Judges Case (2015):

  • 99th CA was declared unconstitutional and NJAC Act was struck down.
  • Collegium System was restored.

Article 125 — Salaries, etc., of Judges

  • Salaries & allowances are determined by Parliament.

Article 126 — Appointment of Acting Chief Justice

President appoints Acting Chief Justice when:

  • Chief Justice's seat is vacant, or
  • Chief Justice is unable to perform duties.
First Female Judge of SC: Justice Fathima Beevi (1989)
No Female Chief Justice of SC till date.

Article 127 — Appointment of Ad Hoc Judges

CJI, with prior consent of the President and in consultation with the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court, may request a High Court judge (qualified for SC) to sit as an ad hoc judge (temporary judge) in the Supreme Court.

Such ad hoc judge enjoys powers, jurisdiction, and privileges of SC judge during the time.

Article 128 — Attendance of Retired Judges

  • Retired SC Judges can be invited to sit and act as Judge of SC.

Article 129 — Supreme Court as a Court of Record

SC is a Court of Record:

  • Its decisions are preserved as legal precedents.
  • Has power to punish for 'Contempt of court.'

Article 130 — Seat of Supreme Court

  • The seat of the Supreme Court is at Delhi.
  • SC can sit elsewhere if CJI recommends and President approves.

Article 131 — Original Jurisdiction of Supreme Court

  • SC has Exclusive Original Jurisdiction in disputes:
  • Between Government of India and one or more States.
  • Between GoI and any state or states on one side and one or more states on the other side.
  • Between two or more States.
Article 131 (A): introduced by 42nd CA, 1976. It granted SC exclusive authority to determine the validity of central laws, it was further repealed by 43rd CA, 1977.

Article 132 — Appellate Jurisdiction of SC (Constitutional Matters)

  • By way of appeal from High Court in Constitutional matters.

Article 133 — Appellate Jurisdiction of SC (Civil Matters)

  • Appeal to SC from HC on judgments in civil cases like: Property, Marriage, Divorce, etc.

Article 134 — Appellate Jurisdiction (Criminal Matters)

Article 135 — Federal Court's Powers

  • SC can exercise powers of the Federal Court under pre-Constitution laws.

Article 136 — Special Leave to Appeal

  • SC can grant Special Leave to appeal from any court/tribunal judgment (except those related to Armed forces courts or Military Tribunals/Courts-martial.)

Article 137 — Review of Judgments

  • SC can review its own judgments or orders.

Article 138 — Enlargement of SC Jurisdiction

  • Parliament may expand SC's jurisdiction by law.

Article 139 — Power to Issue Certain Writs

  • SC can issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights given under Article 32.
  • For other purposes, it requires Parliamentary permission.

Article 140 — Ancillary Powers of Supreme Court

Article 141 — Law Declared by SC to be binding on all Courts

Article 142 — Enforcement of Decrees and Orders

  • SC may pass any decree/order for complete justice.

Article 143 — Advisory Jurisdiction

  • President may refer 2 kinds of matters to SC for advice.
  1. 1. Pre-constitutional matters
  2. 2. Matters of General importance

In pre-constitutional matters, SC must give its advice to President, and in both the cases, the advice is not binding on him.

Article 144 — Civil and Judicial Authorities to Act in Aid of SC

Article 145 — Rules of Court, etc.

  • SC can make its own procedural rules with President's approval as long as it does not conflict with the laws made by the Parliament.

Article 146 — Officers and Servants of the Supreme Court.

  • Appointments: CJI of SC appoints the Court's officers and Staff.
  • Service Conditions: CJI sets the rules for the staff employment and salaries.
  • Expenses: The SC operating cost, like staff salaries, pensions are paid from Consolidated Fund of India.

Article 147 — Interpretation

Constitution clarifies that when interpreting the constitution, any significant legal question should also be considered: GOI Act, 1935, Indian Independence Act, 1947 and related orders and amendments to both of these Acts.

Judicial review borrowed from the U.S. Constitution.

§ 4PART VI - HIGH COURT

[Article 214-231]

Article 214 — Establishment of High Courts

  • Each State shall have a High Court.

Article 215 — High Court to be Court of Record

Article 216 — Constitution of High Courts

  • One Chief Justice and other Judges as Parliament may decide.

Article 217 — Appointment and Conditions of Judges

(1) Appointment of HC Judges is done by the President after consultation with: Chief Justice of India, Governor of State, Chief Justice of the High Court. (Collegium)

  • Maximum age for HC Judge: 62 years
  • HC judge shall hand his resignation to the President.
  • His Removal process is same as that of SC Judge.

(2) Qualifications:

  • 10 years advocate of HC, or
  • 10 years holding judicial office.

No provision for "Distinguished Jurist" in HC.

Article 218 — Application of Certain Provisions

  • Applies SC Judges' removal procedure to HC Judges, Judges Inquiry Act, 1968.

Article 219 — Oath or Affirmation

  • HC Judges take oath before the Governor.

Article 220 — Restriction on Practice After Retirement

  • Former HC judges cannot practice law before any court except: SC & other HCs.

Article 221 — Salaries and Allowances

  • Salaries and allowances are drawn from Consolidated Fund of State while Pensions are drawn from Consolidated Fund of India.
  • Salaries, allowances, leaves and pension rights are determined by the Parliament.

Article 222 — Transfer of Judges

  • President can transfer HC judges after consultation with CJI.

Article 223 — Appointment of Acting Chief Justice

The President can appoint an Acting Chief Justice when:

  • The office of the Chief Justice of the High Court is vacant, or
  • The Chief Justice is unable to perform duties due to absence or any other reason.

Article 224 — Appointment of Additional and Acting Judges

(1) Additional Judges: If the workload of High Court increases (e.g. due to arrears), the President may appoint additional judges for a temporary period not exceeding 2 years.

(2) Acting Judges: If a judge is absent, unable to perform duties, or seat is vacant, the President may appoint an acting judge.

  • These appointments to be done in consultation with CJI.

Article 224A — Appointment of Retired Judges at Sittings of High Courts

The Chief Justice of a HC can request the attendance of a retired judge of that HC or any other HC.

Article 225 — Jurisdiction of HC:

  • Original jurisdiction - revenue matters, election disputes of MPs and MLAs.
  • Appellate jurisdiction - hear appeals about decisions made by lower courts.
  • Writ jurisdiction.

Article 226 — Power of HC to Issue Writs

  • HC has wider writ jurisdiction than SC.
  • It can issue writs on Legal + Fundamental Rights.
  • HC may refuse to issue writ, SC cannot.

Article 227 — Superintendence over Subordinate Courts

Article 228 — Transfer of Certain Cases to HC

Article 229 — Officers and Servants of HC - by Chief Justice of HC.

Article 230 — Extension of Jurisdiction to Union Territories: Power of Parliament —

  • Andaman & Nicobar → Calcutta HC
  • Lakshadweep → Kerala HC
  • Puducherry → Madras HC
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli & Daman and Diu → Maharashtra HC
  • Chandigarh → Punjab and Haryana HC

Article 231

  • Establishment of Common High Court for two or more States. (7th CA, 1956) for example:

a. Maharashtra and Goa have a common HC at Mumbai, Maharashtra.

b. Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram and Assam have a common HC at Guwahati, Assam.

Article 232 — Transfer of Cases to Federal Court (Repealed)

By the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956.

1st HC (1862): Calcutta High Court.
1st Female HC Judge: Justice Anna Chandy (Kerala).
1st Female Chief Justice of HC: Justice Leila Seth (Himachal Pradesh)
Total High Courts in India: 25

§ 5SUBORDINATE COURTS

Article 233 — Appointment of District Judges

(1) District Judge to be appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court.

(2) A person not already in the service of the Union or of the State shall only be eligible to be appointed a district judge if he has been for not less than seven years an advocate or a pleader and is recommended by the High Court for appointment.

Article 233A — Validation of Appointments of District Judges.

Article 234 — Recruitment of Persons Other than District Judges to the Judicial Services shall be made by the Governor of the state.

Article 235 — Control Over Subordinate Courts.
